title: wielding man told cops to shoot, inquest hears - Winnipeg Free Press
subtitle: Breaking News, Sports, Manitoba, Canada
article: Hey there, time traveller!
This article was published 24/06/2009 (5911 days ago), so information in it may no longer be current.
IN one hand, the crying man held a kitchen knife.
In the other arm, he grabbed his 11-year-old daughter.
A trained hostage negotiator stood at the bottom of the Alfred Avenue staircase and pleaded for minutes with Howard Fleury to drop the knife.
But the negotiator, Sgt. Maurice Rioux, testified at an inquest Tuesday he wasn't successful in subduing Fleury, and Fleury screamed repeatedly at police to shoot him.
The young girl slipped away from her father's grip into a nearby bedroom upstairs where two diapered two-year-olds sat on a mattress.
Fleury then charged towards police down a staircase at 339 Alfred Ave., according to officers who saw and heard the confrontation.
Two officers near Rioux fired a series of gunshots into Fleury's chest and killed him.

Four officers who responded to a high-priority domestic dispute at 339 Alfred between Fleury and his estranged common-law wife, Kimberly Desjarlais, spoke Tuesday at the second day of the inquest into the shooting death of Fleury, 34, on on Dec. 2, 2005
Police said that after Fleury's death, they covered the children with blankets and carried them over their father's body to a local police detachment.
There, the 11-year-old changed into a paper shirt because her own pajama top was smeared with blood.
"Our objective was to get all the children out," said Rioux, now retired from the Winnipeg Police Service. "I've never seen anger and focus like that."
Each officer called at the inquest said police had no choice but to shoot the armed man while children remained in the home.
Officers testified that when the shooting occurred, Fleury's common-law wife and at least five children were in the home's basement while three remained upstairs.
Rioux said the decision by police to shoot Fleury was a matter of public safety.
When lawyer Ian Garber asked why police didn't retreat and let Fleury calm himself, Rixous replied: "I would have done that had there been no children in the house."

Rioux, a 37-year police veteran, told Judge Catherine Carlson it was the only time in his career he had been at a police-involved shooting. About six weeks before, Rioux said, he had successfully persuaded an intoxicated, violent man to put down a knife.
Rioux testified that Fleury repeatedly referred to "suicide by cop" while he argued with police.
An attempt to pepper-spray Fleury failed to stop him, said Rioux. Instead, he said it drove Fleury to climb back up the staircase on his hands and knees before he began weeping.
"He started talking about 'no one will hire me. No one will give me a job,'" said Rioux.
Rioux retired only months after Fleury died.
The inquest continues today.
